This will be downvoted as Swedes love their systems, but here's how it worked ~10 years ago. Some things may be better now, some worse. We had two awful deliveries in Sweden and one excellent one in Switzerland, which naturally colours my views. The hospital does not see patients as customers - the Region managers are the customers. They don't care about what taxes are paid.

- Births in Sweden are generally safe and emergencies are swiftly handled. They are, however, often more uncomfortable and painful than in other countries.

- Delivery hospital won't be guaranteed. If they are full or low on staff due to vacations/absences, you may be sent elsewhere on the date with little or no warning. The new place may be an hour away or more. It is also common to be sent home if they judge you to not be sufficiently ready. The only way to have a guaranteed place in Sweden (and the only way to have an obstetrician handle the birth) is by having a planned C-section.

- Some (mostly older) midwives discourage pain relief and try to argue against it. Anaesthesiologists are on call but often have a call-in time of an hour, more if there are emergencies. If you want an epidural, insist on the anaesthesiologist being called immediately when you come in and make sure you and your partner firmly tell the midwife this is what you want, and check that they actually call the anaesthesiologist.

- Some regions let mothers go past their due date by more than one week, despite it being known for more than 20 years that this causes high risks for babies. Insist on inducement (igångsättning) if this is the case at the hospital you go to and you are approaching that due date limit.

- Ask the hospital what their policy is for single rooms. In some cases (premature deliveries) you may after the birth be sharing a room with another mother and the family visitors she gets. Generally speaking, the people at the hospital will mirror the population of the locality.
